title: Thermodynamic–kinetic calculations and dilatometric verification of the martensitic and bainitic transformations in 4% medium-Mn steel
abstract: Abstract The present study investigated the theoretical and experimental phase transitions phenomena during continuous cooling and isothermal holding above and below M s  temperature in 4 mass. % Mn medium-Mn steel. The thermodynamic–kinetic calculations were performed using JMatPro software, and phase transformations were recorded using a BÄHR high-resolution DIL805A/D dilatometer. The research covered continuous cooling rates from 60 to 0.05 °C s –1  and isothermal holding temperatures in a range between 420 °C and 230 °C. The issues related to both modelling and dilatometric methodology were discussed. The CCT and TTT diagrams were prepared on the basis of dilatometry and compared with the results of light microscopy and hardness tests. The alloy containing about 4 mass.% Mn and 0.22% Mo exhibited very high hardenability as only continuous cooling with rates lower than 1 °C s –1  allowed the bainitic transformation to be initiated. The bainitic transformation is accelerated after passing the M s  temperature. Both the incubation time and the time needed to complete the transformation were significantly reduced (the incubation time from 100 s to below 1 s and the completion time from over 4000 s to below 1000 s). The obtained microstructures were homogeneous and refined.
journal: Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A cooling rate from the austenitization and isothermal holding (IH) temperature have a decisive influence on produced microstructures and mechanical properties of advanced medium-Mn steels [ 1 ]: bainitic [ 2 ] and quenching and partitioning (Q&P) [ 3 ] steels. In both cases, ferritic and/or pearlitic transformations during cooling are not beneficial because they produce microstructures of low strength and ductility. Therefore, it is necessary to perform the cooling at a rate higher than critical. Second important parameter during cooling of both mentioned types of advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) is the isothermal holding temperature [ 4 ].

In case of bainitic steels an IH temperature determines a grain size of bainitic plates and the fraction and size of retained austenite (RA) [ 5 ]. Microstructure refinement controls strength properties of the material while the fraction and size of retained austenite control plasticity, toughness and fatigue resistance. With the decrease in isothermal holding temperature of bainitic steels the microstructure is refined, leading to an increase in yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS). However, its plastic properties like uniform (UEl) and total elongation (TEl) decrease and less RA may be obtained [ 6 ].

For Q&P steels, a temperature of incomplete quenching, which is the first isothermal holding step in their heat treatment route, is crucial for final mechanical properties [ 3 ]. If quenching is stopped at too high temperature a formed fraction of martensite is low, which does not allow to enrich in carbon the remaining fraction of austenite during the partitioning stage. It results in a severe martensitic transformation during final cooling [ 7 ]. The microstructure of Q&P steel should consist of tempered martensite guaranteed high strength and about 15% of RA, which improves plasticity and toughness. If a high fraction of austenite transforms into martensite during final cooling the microstructure comprises also fresh martensite, which due to its brittleness decreases significantly the steel’s plasticity. Hase et al. [ 8 ] showed that ductility and fracture toughness were improved by eliminating fresh martensite from the microstructure. On the other hand, if quenching is stopped at too low temperature, the high fraction of formed martensite decreases a final fraction of RA, which decreases the steel’s plasticity.

The change in isothermal holding/quenching stop temperature influences also the kinetics of further transformations [ 9 ], which in case of bainitic steels determines the process duration and in case of Q&P steels may affect the final microstructure. If bainite is formed from the austenite during incomplete quenching, a final fraction of RA will be limited. Therefore, the characterization of both the influence of cooling rate and the isothermal holding temperature is crucial for designing heat treatment routes of the newest generation of AHSS steels—medium-Mn steels [ 1 ,  10 ].

The present work aims at analysing the phase transformation kinetics in 4Mn steel using thermodynamic calculations and dilatometry. The investigated steel was initially characterized using modelling and thermodynamic–kinetic calculations and next subjected to dilatometric tests characterized by a number of isothermal holdings in a bainitic transformation range, both above and below the martensite start (M s ) temperature. The effect of martensite on the kinetics of bainitic transformation and resulting morphology and phase composition of the alloy was investigated.

sections.heading: Materials and methods
paragraphs: The chemical composition of the steel investigated is listed in Table  1 . The carbon level was limited to < 0.2 mass/% to not deteriorate the machinability of steel. The Mn level of about 4% was added to improve hardenability and stabilize RA. Si and Al are crucial additions for bainitic and Q&P steels containing retained austenite as they inhibit carbide precipitation during isothermal holding. Therefore, carbon present in a solid solution can enrich austenite instead of being trapped in carbides. Mo addition was added to improve hardenability and solid solution strengthening of the steel. The microadditions of Ti and V were added to refine prior austenite grains, which improves strength properties of the steel. Table 1 Chemical composition of investigated medium-Mn steel Chemical element C Mn Si Al Mo Ti V Mass/% 0.17 3.92 1.02 0.53 0.22 0.032 0.069

The steel was cast in a vacuum furnace under argon atmosphere into ingots of 100 kg. The cast ingot was austenitized at 1200 °C for 2 h in order to homogenize the chemical composition. Afterwards, the material was hot-rolled in the temperature range of 1200–900 °C to a thickness of ~ 22 mm using the LPS/B semi-industrial line (Łukasiewicz Research Network–Upper Silesian Institute of Technology, Gliwice, Poland). The thermodynamic calculations including producing equilibrium diagrams, and CCT, and TTT diagrams and determining phase transformations kinetics were performed using JMatPro v14.1. The verification of the influence of cooling rate and isothermal holding temperature was performed using BÄHR high-resolution dilatometer DIL805A/D. The dilatometry data was analysed according to ASTM A1033-04. The austempering and Q&P treatment may be performed both as individual processes or be integrated with hot working. In this study the dilatometric tests were performed using undeformed samples. The cylindrical dilatometric samples with the diameter of 4 mm and length of 10 mm were machined from the hot-rolled material. The dilatometric investigations were performed in vacuum. The material was cooled using helium and a specimen temperature was measured and controlled using a S-type thermocouple welded to the central part of the length of the sample. First, heating and cooling processes were performed to determine A c1 , A c3  and M s  temperatures of the alloy. The initial heating was selected to be 200 °C/h in order to approach equilibrium conditions. For further tests a heating rate was set to 10 °C s –1 , and an austenization temperature to 1100 °C. The cooling was performed in the range from 60 to 0.05 °C s –1 . After characterization of the phase transformation kinetics during continuous cooling, the experiments of isothermal holding were performed at a final cooling rate of 1 °C s –1 . The isothermal holdings were performed in the temperature range from 450 °C to 230 °C, which covered both the temperatures above and below M s .

After the dilatometric tests, the samples were cut in half of the length, grinded using SiC paper with a grid up to 1200, and polished using diamond pasts with 3 μm and 1 μm particle grain sizes. The final polishing was performed using 35 nm colloidal silica to ensure a flat surface with minimal deformation. For microstructural observations the samples were etched using 3% nital for ~ 4 s at room temperature. The microstructure of steel was investigated using a Zeiss Observer Z1m light microscope.

The hardness of heat-treated samples was measured using a Future-Tech FM-700 Vickers hardness tester at a load of 1 kgf. Twelve measurements for each sample were taken. The extreme values were discarded and the average value of the remaining measurements was calculated.

sections.heading: Phase transitions during continuous heating and cooling
paragraphs: The first step during analysing a new alloy is to characterize its critical temperatures: A c1  and A c3  temperatures during continuous heating and austenite decomposition temperatures like M s  during continuous cooling. Figure  1 a presents the temperature evolution of the phases under equilibrium conditions. According to the simulations, the A c1  temperature of the alloy, where austenite starts to form is about 596 °C. Up to this temperature, the alloy’s microstructure is composed of ferrite and below 2% of carbides. Typical carbides like cementite are present in the microstructure up to the temperature of 713 °C. Above this temperature, only the stable carbides containing microadditions of Ti and V (M(C, N)) are present in the microstructure up to about 1115 °C, which fraction does not exceed 0.15%. The ferrite is completely transformed into austenite at 835 °C, which is the A c3  temperature. Therefore, according to the simulations the austenitization temperature should be at least 860 °C. Fig. 1 Temperature evolution of the phases during heating determined using  a  thermodynamic simulations (JMatPro software), and  b  dilatometry

The theoretical results should be always validated experimentally. To determine real A c1  and A c3  temperatures, the dilatometry was used (Fig.  1 b). The α to γ transformation is accompanied by the sample contraction as the lattice parameter for austenite is smaller than for ferrite. This phenomenon is used to determine a point where transformation begins as the sample starts to shrink, which is visible in sample’s relative change in length (RCL) results (Fig.  1 b). The completion of austenitization is also recognizable as changes in thermal expansion return to a linear form again [ 11 ]. According to the literature, with increasing heating rate critical temperatures may also increase even by several dozen °C [ 12 ]. In order to approach equilibrium conditions, these types of tests are usually carried out at a heating rate of 200 °C/h [ 13 ], which was done also in our experiment. The dilatometric results indicate that the A c1  and A c3  temperatures of the analysed alloy are 705 °C and 908 °C, respectively. It is visible that the theoretical results differ significantly from the experimental ones, especially for the A c1  temperature (difference of 109 °C). Results presented in other works [ 14 ,  15 ] also indicate that the accuracy of the currently available models for medium-Mn steels needs to be further improved due to complex chemistry of novel ferrous alloys.

Another important characteristic of the steel is the phase transformation kinetics during cooling. To create the continuous-cooling-transformation (CCT) diagram, which summarizes temperatures and a type of transformations taking place in the material, the dilatometric tests of continuous cooling should be carried out. Figure  2  presents both the theoretical and dilatometric approaches to this issue, in a form of linear expansion changes as a function of temperature. The γ to α transformations like ferritic, pearlitic, bainitic and martensitic ones are related to sample expansion, clearly recognizable in dilatograms (Fig.  2 ). Results obtained from simulations (Fig.  2 a) show that due to the high hardenability of analysed steel caused by Mn and Mo, only at cooling rates lower than 1 °C s –1  the ferritic and pearlitic transformations take place at a temperature range of 600–550 °C. At a cooling rate of 1 °C s –1  the bainitic transformation starts at ~ 400 °C, and with a further decrease in the temperature the martensitic transformation begins at 296 °C. At a cooling rate of 60 °C s –1 , only the martensitic transformation takes place. It starts at the temperature of 296 °C, which is the theoretical M s  temperature of the alloy. For the experimental results, only martensitic transformation is recorded in samples cooled at a rate ≤ 0.5 °C s –1 , which indicates higher hardenability of the steel in comparison to the simulations. The bainitic transformation takes place in samples cooled at a rate of 0.1 °C s –1  and 0.05 °Cs –1 . For these two cooling rates, also an abnormal thermal linear expansion is visible at about 610 °C. It should be usually identified as ferritic/pearlitic transformation; however, for medium-Mn steels with a similar Mn concentration, the ferritic and pearlitic transformation do not occur at such cooling rates [ 16 ]. This issue is analysed in detail later in the article. Fig. 2 Linear expansion changes (and respective phase transformations) of samples during cooling at different cooling rates in the range from 60 °C s –1  to 0.05 °C s –1  determined using  a  thermodynamic–kinetic simulations (JMatPro software), and  b  dilatometry

Figure  3  presents the direct comparison of computational (JMatPro) and dilatometric results at a cooling rate of 10 °C s –1 . The slope of the plotted results representing thermal expansion coefficient and a sample expansion related to the martensitic transformation are consistent. However, the M s  temperature differs as it is 63 °C higher for dilatometric results. For the dilatometry the transformation is more gradual, while the simulations indicate a very rapid transformation at its beginning. Both in case of heating and cooling the theoretical results are shifted to lower temperatures in comparison to the physical experiments, which indicates the need to change the influence factor of Mn on phase transformations in the current JMatPro model. Fig. 3 Comparison of linear expansion changes during cooling the samples from 1100 °C at a cooling rate of 10 °C s –1  for thermodynamic–kinetic simulations (JMatPro software) and dilatometry

In order to clearly identify a type of phase transformations taking place in the material during cooling, the dilatometric results should be compared with microstructure images and hardness results. Light microscopy images (Fig.  4 ) indicate that bainite is present in samples cooled at rates of 0.05 and 0.1 °C s –1 , which is consistent with the dilatometry. Bainite may be recognized by the morphology of fine plates arranged parallel to each other in the form of packets. In these samples, the matrix is composed of fine martensite in the form of laths or lenticular grains, which are visibly thicker than bainite. The formation of martensite was also recorded by dilatometry. However, at cooling rates of 0.05 and 0.1 °C s –1  an expansion of the sample was also recorded at a temperature of approximately 610 °C, which however is not represented in the microstructure. Samples cooled at a rate > 0.1 °C s –1  exhibit microstructures composed of martensite. No other phase was observed. It is also visible that the microstructure is more fragmented with an increase in the cooling rate due to the shorter residence time at a high temperature and therefore, a smaller growth of the parent austenite grain. The hardness results also confirm the dilatometric results (Fig.  5 ). The hardness is at a similar level of ~ 440 HV1 up to a cooling rate of 0.5 °C s –1 . For slower cooling, hardness decreases as the softer bainite is formed in the microstructure. The slight decrease in hardness of ~ 15 HV1 with a decrease in cooling rate for samples cooled at rates 60–0.5 °C s –1  is probably caused by the more extent self-tempering effect of the martensitic sample due to slower cooling. Fig. 4 Light microscopy images of samples cooled at different rates  a  0.05 °C s –1 ,  b  0.1 °C s –1 ,  c  0.5 °C s –1 ,  d  60 °C s –1 Fig. 5 Changes in hardness as a function of cooling rate of analysed steel from 60 °C s –1  to 0.05 °C s –1

The thermodynamic–kinetic calculations and combined results of dilatometry, light microscopy and hardness measurements allowed to create the final CCT diagrams (Fig.  6 ). For the experimental results (Fig.  6 b) the influence of Mn and Mo on hardenability of steel is more expressed than in case of the thermodynamic–kinetic simulations (Fig.  6 a). Only the bainitic and martensitic transformations were recorded up to a cooling rate of only 0.05 °C s –1 . The ferritic and pearlitic transformations were not recorded despite the thermodynamic–kinetic simulations suggesting that they should be present already for a sample cooled at a rate of 0.1 °C s –1 . The differences in M s  temperatures were already mentioned in the text; however, the difference is also visible in case of M f  temperature, which is ~ 10 °C higher for the experimental approach. For samples where the bainitic transformation took place, the M f  temperature increases as part of austenite was transformed to bainite prior to martensitic transformation, which causes it to occur in a smaller range and thus is completed at a higher temperature.

sections.heading: Abnormal linear expansion during cooling
paragraphs: The dilatometric sample expansions, which were recorded during cooling at rates of 0.1 and 0.05 °C s –1  at about 610 °C were not confirmed as ferritic/pearlitic transformations by standard microscopic observations or hardness tests. For this reason, a more detailed analysis of dilatometric results was performed. Beside time, temperature and linear expansion, the dilatometry provides a number of different variables, which allows to identify the origin of any distortions in the results. In our case, the records regarding the cooling process turned out to be useful. In order to avoid surface oxidation, the tests were performed in a vacuum. Due to the need for cooling at a constant rate, helium was used to regulate it, which is a standard procedure in dilatometric tests. In the first cooling stage, regulation of the induction generator allows maintaining a constant cooling rate. However, at some point the gas blowing is started—the impact of which is then measured using a thermocouple and the device adjusts its intensity to the given conditions. The first hit of gas on a sample may cause sample vibration resulting in measurement inaccuracy [ 11 ]. During cooling, there is also a slight temperature gradient in the sample as the device measures only the surface temperature of the sample as a thermocouple is placed there. Turning on the gas flow itself also affects the loss of vacuum in the test chamber, which may also result in measurement disruptions. Hence, disturbances in the dilatometric curve related to the start of gas cooling and the loss of vacuum in the test chamber were recorded during dilatometric tests (Fig.  7 ). The slower the cooling rate, both of these phenomena occur at a lower temperature. When cooling was carried out at a rate of 60 °C s –1  (Fig.  7 d), the gas is activated almost immediately, resulting in a distorted curve at temperatures above 1000 °C. In the case of samples cooled at rates of 0.1 °C s –1  and 0.05 °C s –1 , this effect occurs at a temperature of about 610 °C (Fig.  7 a, b). The results in Fig.  7 c, d also clearly show that the martensitic transformation is an exothermic process [ 17 ,  18 ]. From the moment the martensitic transformation began, the gas flow was significantly increased by the dilatometer to maintain a constant cooling rate, which indicates the process of heat release in the sample (Fig.  7 ). Fig. 6 CCT diagrams determined using  a  thermodynamic simulations (JMatPro software), and  b  experimentally by dilatometry, hardness measurements and light microscopy Fig. 7 The influence of the sample cooling rate on beginning the gas flow and the loss of vacuum in the test chamber

The impinging flow of the quenching gas may cause local dilatometric inaccuracy. However, after the cooling conditions stabilize, the slope of the dilatometric curve should return to its previous value, which was not recorded in the tests. For this reason, the microstructures of the samples were analysed but at much lower magnifications. The tests showed that in samples cooled at rates of 0.1 °C s –1  and 0.05 °C s –1  the surface layer shows a large fraction of ferrite (Fig.  8 a), while the core of the sample is composed of martensite and bainite as described earlier. In the case of samples cooled at rates of 0.5—60 °C s –1  the entire cross section of the dilatometric sample is uniform (Fig.  8 b). The phenomenon of ferrite formation occurring in very slowly cooled samples can be only explained by the decarburization process of the material despite vacuum atmosphere and helium cooling were used to prevent oxidation decarburization of the ferrous material. The decarburized layer with a ferritic structure is approximately 400 μm thick. For a sample with a diameter of 4 mm and a length of 10 mm the ferritic transformation took place in approximately 40% of the material volume, which could result in linear expansion and a change in linear expansion coefficient (curve slope) [ 19 ] recorded by the dilatometer. The superimposition of both disturbances caused by the activation of the gas supply and the ferritic transformation at the surface explain the observed trends in the dilatometric curves for the slowest cooled samples. Due to the fact that these phenomena result mainly from the testing methodology it should not be taken into account during creating and analysing the CCT diagram of the tested material. Fig. 8 The influence of cooling rate on near-surface phase composition:  a  0.05 °C s –1 ,  b  0.5 °C s –1

sections.heading: Isothermal holding above and below M s  temperature
paragraphs: Investigations concerning continuous cooling of samples at different rates allowed to determine M s  and M f  temperatures and a critical cooling rate allowed to avoid other transformations than martensitic. The results were used to design heat treatment parameters allowing to analyse the influence of the prior martensitic transformation on bainitic transformation in analysed steel. Such a situation where martensite is formed in the initial step of heat treatment can be present during austempering or Q&P treatment. Therefore, its influence on phase transformation kinetics and microstructure has to be analysed, which may be performed using the time–temperature-transformation (TTT) diagram. Figure  9  presents the dilatometric cooling and isothermal holding results at different temperatures above and below M s  temperature for computational (Fig.  9 a) and experimental (Fig.  9 b) approaches. The dilatometric results in Fig.  9  are shown as a function of temperature. Therefore, the martensitic transformation is presented as a curve because it occurs with a temperature change, and the bainitic transformation is represented by a vertical line as it is accompanied by sample expansion and occurs at a constant temperature. Initial research indicated that the material model used by JMatPro software resulted in underestimation of the M s  temperature compared to experimental studies by approximately 60 °C. For this reason, the results of both methods cannot be directly compared but some trends of changes with a decrease in the isothermal holding temperature can be analysed. Results of modelling present in Fig.  9 a assume that despite the temperature of isothermal holding changes, the post-holding expansion of the sample is almost equal. It means that above the M s  temperature all austenite should be transformed into bainite and below M s  temperature, part of austenite is transformed to martensite and next a remaining fraction of austenite is transformed to bainite. Therefore, the theoretical calculations do not take into account the T 0  rule [ 5 ,  20 ], where both the kinetics and the range of the bainitic transformation are controlled by the isothermal holding temperature and a carbon content in the austenite. With a decrease in isothermal holding temperature, austenite of higher carbon content may be transformed into bainite, while at a higher IH temperature the same austenite remains stable. It is clearly shown in experimental results in Fig.  9 b, where at temperatures above 400 °C the bainitic transformation barely occurred. At such high temperatures, the bainite fraction will not exceed some level regardless of the isothermal holding time, and will transform eventually to martensite during final cooling. With a decrease in the isothermal holding temperature the transformation is more advanced. If the temperature decreases below the M s  temperature, the martensitic transformation takes place. However, as the isothermal holding is performed between M s  and M f  temperatures, a remaining fraction of austenite transforms eventually to bainite during isothermal holding. Fig. 9 Linear expansion changes of samples during cooling and isothermal holding at different temperatures determined using  a  thermodynamic–kinetic simulations using JMatPro software, and  b  dilatometry; IH – isothermal holding

The linear expansion as a function of time showing the bainitic transformation kinetics is present in Fig.  10 . In case of the theoretical calculations (Fig.  10 a) at the highest temperature of isothermal holding (450 °C), the transformation starts after ~ 106 s, which is the incubation time. With decreasing the holding temperature to 400 °C the incubation time is reduced to ~ 35 s and the transformation is much more dynamic, especially in the initial 200 s. With a further decrease in the temperature of isothermal holding the incubation time increases again up to 233 s at 300 °C, which is 4 °C above the M s  temperature. Below 400 °C the kinetics of bainitic transformation decreases. At 270 °C, which is the first variant below M s  the incubation time increases up to over 400 s, and the bainitic transformation kinetics further decreases. With decrease in the isothermal temperature to 230 °C, which is 60 °C higher than the theoretical M f  temperature, during the 1500 s of analysis the bainitic transformation did not start. For the experimental results (Fig.  10 b) for decreasing the isothermal holding temperature from 420 to 390 °C the incubation time decreases from about 1300 to 100 s, and the transformation is more advanced. With a further drop of holding temperature to 370 °C (slightly above M s ) the incubation time again increases to about 300 s. However, the sample expansion related to bainitic transformation increases. This is in good agreement with the literature and T 0  rule, where with a decrease in holding temperature more austenite may be transformed to bainite [ 5 ,  20 ]. If the isothermal holding is performed below M s  temperature, the incubation time is reduced almost to 0 s. The transformation starts rapidly in all the range of IH between M s  and M f  temperatures. However, with a decrease in temperature the linear expansion related to bainitic transformation decreases as more austenite is transformed initially to martensite. At isothermal holding at 230 °C, which is only ~ 40 °C higher than the M f  temperature of the alloy, the bainitic transformation starts almost immediately and is completed in time shorter than 1000 s. It shows that the martensitic transformation reduces significantly the incubation time and time needed to complete bainitic transformation [ 21 ]. The comparison of the theoretical and experimental results (Fig.  10 ) beside a change in bainitic transformation kinetics shows also that the linear expansion related to bainitic transformation recorded by dilatometry is significantly lower compared to the calculations and it reaches up to 0.5% and 0.3%, respectively. Fig. 10 Linear expansion changes of samples during isothermal holding at different temperatures determined using  a  thermodynamic–kinetic simulations using JMatPro software, and  b  dilatometry

The results of light microscopy confirm the dilatometric observations (Fig.  11 ). At high isothermal holding temperatures the microstructure is composed mainly of martensite, which was formed during final cooling. Only a small island of bainitic morphology was observed (Fig.  11 a). With a decrease in isothermal holding temperature more bainite is formed in the microstructure (Fig.  11 b,c). After holding at 370 °C almost all microstructure is composed of bainite, and only small martensitic regions were observed (Fig.  11 c). In case of samples isothermally held below the M s  temperature the microstructure is very refined and homogenous. The experimental results indicate that it should be composed of martensite and bainite; however, it is impossible to distinguish both phases (Fig.  11 d). Fig. 11 Light microscopy images for samples isothermally held at different temperatures:  a  400 °C,  b  390 °C,  c  370 °C,  d  250 °C (below M s  temperature)

The hardness results (Fig.  12 ) indicate that at the highest isothermal holding temperatures (> 400 °C) hardness is at a constant level of about 465 HV1, which is related to the microstructure composed of martensite and only small fraction of bainite. With a further decrease in isothermal holding temperature to 310 °C a significant decrease in hardness to ~ 94HV1 is visible due to an increasing fraction of softer bainite in the microstructure. At the isothermal holdings below M s  an increase in hardness is observed (up to 430 HV1 at 230 °C), which is related again to an increasing fraction of martensite formed prior to the isothermal holding. Also with decreasing the isothermal holding bainite tends to improve its hardness [ 22 ] because the formed laths have smaller thickness [ 23 ,  24 ]. Fig. 12 Changes in hardness depending on the isothermal holding temperature of analysed steel from 420 °C to 230 °C

The final TTT diagrams present in Fig.  13  show differences between the theoretical and experimental results. It should be noted that for theoretical results the bainitic bay is in a range of about 160 °C, while for experimental results it is only about 50 °C. For the theoretical results the incubation time is also significantly shorter. Initially with a decrease in isothermal holding temperature the incubation time and time required to complete bainitic transformation decrease, which is in good agreement between both methods and literature [ 25 ]. Next, due to a decreasing temperature of isothermal holding the incubation time and kinetics of bainitic transformation decrease which is also in good agreement. The differences are noted below the M s  temperature, where for the theoretical results obtained using the JMatPro software the tendency of increasing incubation time and decreasing transformation kinetics continues. In case of experimental results the significant acceleration of the transformation is visible in comparison to the isothermal holding performed slightly above M s  temperature. The incubation time is almost not present and the time needed to complete the transformation is shorter than for samples held above the M s  temperature. Fig. 13 TTT diagrams determined using  a  thermodynamic–kinetic simulations using JMatPro software, and  b  experimentally using dilatometry, hardness measurements and light microscopy

sections.heading: Influence of the obtained results on modern heat treatment of AHSS
paragraphs: The obtained results are very important in case of designing new heat treatment cycles for modern AHSS. First of all, the theoretical results obtained using a current database implemented in JMatPro software cannot be taken directly because there are significant differences in comparison to the experimental ones. Therefore, when working on the development or optimization of heat treatment, one can only rely roughly on the tendency of changes depending on temperature or time in case of theoretical results. The theoretical results for isothermal holding below M s  temperatures are completely inconsistent with the experimental results.

The kinetics of martensitic transformation and bainitic transformation below M s  temperature are crucial for designing austempering below M s  temperature (Fig.  14 a) and Q&P treatment (Fig.  14 b). In case of austempering, decreasing the isothermal holding temperature influences the refinement of the microstructure and reduction in the bainite plate thickness. This phenomenon results in increased hardness and toughness of the material [ 22 ]. However, with decreasing temperature the incubation time and completion time of bainitic transformation are significantly increased (from 134 s at 390 °C to over 440 s at 360 °C). Our investigations show that reducing the isothermal holding temperature below the M s  temperature of the alloy allows to reduce drastically the incubation time to below 2 s and the time needed to complete bainitic transformation even in comparison to the typical holding temperatures (from over 4300 s at 380 °C to about 4200 s at 310 °C). However, the martensitic transformation prior to bainitic holding may cause some formation of coarse martensitic laths [ 26 ,  27 ], which may deteriorate mechanical properties of steel [ 26 ]. Such coarse martensite was not observed in our study because the microstructures generated below M s  temperature show high refinement and homogeneity (Fig.  11 d). In case of Q&P process the initial incomplete quenching is aimed to transform about 80% of austenite into martensite. However, the remaining 20% should not transform to bainite or martensite as it is supposed to be stabilized during a next partitioning step [ 27 ,  28 ]. As our investigations showed, the bainitic transformation after incomplete martensitic transformation (Fig.  10 b) occurs very rapidly. It suggests that the post-quenching holding in the Q&P treatment should be short, and the temperature should be increased to the partition level rapidly. Fig. 14 Proposed schemes of  a  austempering and  b  Q&P heat treatments

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The investigations concerned the thermodynamic–kinetic simulation and experimental verification of phase transitions during continuous cooling and isothermal holding above and below M s  temperature in advanced 0.17C-3.92Mn-1.02Si-0.53Al-0.22Mo-0.032Ti-0.069 V medium-Mn alloy. It was found that: In case of medium-Mn steel, currently the thermodynamic–kinetic simulations can only be used to estimate the results and indicate some trends in phase transformation behaviour of the alloy but it is still necessary to optimize the chemical composition and heat treatment using experimental methods, especially regarding bainitic transformation taking place after prior martensite transformation. Methodology issues like surface decarburization leading to abnormal ferrite formation or an effect of activating cooling gas may affect some distortions in dilatometric results. The addition of about 4% Mn and 0.22% Mo provides high hardenability, so during continuous cooling only in case of cooling rate lower than 0.5 °C s –1  the bainite was formed. At slow cooling rates self-tempering of martensite occurs that was confirmed by a decrease in steel hardness. Martensitic transformation prior to isothermal holding significantly reduces the incubation time (from 134 s at 390 °C to below 2 s s at 310 °C) and completion time of bainitic transformation (from over 4300 s at 380 °C to 4200 s at 310 °C). The influence of martensitic transformation on kinetics of bainitic transformation has to be taken into consideration especially in designing advanced heat treatments like austempering and Q&P.
